strengths: Novel, well-motivated dataset addressing a real problem in multilingual government websites; first document-level cross-lingual RSD benchmark with human annotations

Comprehensive evaluation across diverse model types (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoders) revealing substantial performance gaps (up to 78-point Spearman drop) between synthetic and naturalistic data
Clear, impactful findings: demonstrates LLM failures on long documents, formatting errors, underlabeling; shows unsupervised DiffAlign surprisingly robust
Rigorous dataset construction with detailed guidelines, trial phase feedback, interactive annotation interface, and systematic quality control filtering
Excellent reproducibility with released code/data and comprehensive documentation (appendices, prompts, implementation details); honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Significant annotation quality concerns: inconsistent inter-annotator agreement across language pairs (EN-DE IoU 11.17% vs EN-IT 32.10%), only 2 annotators, only 25 of 224 documents overlap-validated, subjective annotation strategies documented but unresolved (whole phrase vs minimal labeling, omission handling divergence)

Limited generalizability: only high-resource, closely-related European languages with Latin scripts and English-centric pairs; government domain specificity; unclear transfer to other languages, scripts, or domains

Experimental design weaknesses: (1) unequal training data (LLMs 560 augmentations vs encoders 10,000), (2) asymmetric LLM evaluation on SwissGov due to computational constraints, (3) no specified train/test split for the main SwissGov-RSD dataset, (4) label projection validated on only 50 samples with 34-46% sample-level edits
No methodological novelty: applies existing techniques (DiffAlign, LLM prompting, standard fine-tuning); contribution primarily dataset-focused without algorithmic advances

Dataset size modest for modern standards (224 documents); sparse overlap annotation assessment (25 pairs); unresolved questions about EN-DE vs EN-IT agreement gap (3× difference); moderate label correlations especially for EN-DE (66.16% for fuzzy ≥50%)

strengths: Addresses a practical need with a naturalistic cross-lingual dataset based on real government documents, motivated by genuine use cases
Comprehensive benchmarking of diverse systems (12+ LLMs, encoder models, unsupervised approaches) with careful implementation details
Transparent reporting of limitations including annotation disagreements, faulty documents, and annotator discrepancies in Appendix A.4
Excellent reproducibility with released code, data, detailed annotation guidelines, prompts, and supplementary results
Significant finding that synthetic datasets (iSTS-RSD) substantially overestimate performance on naturalistic data (performance gaps up to 78 points)
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement critically low, especially for EN-DE (F1 of 18.09 and 17.22), making the benchmark unreliable for comparing systems; Table 7 shows system rankings differ drastically depending on which annotator's labels are used

Annotation methodology problematic: only 2 annotators (undergraduate/bachelor's students without domain expertise), only 25 overlapping documents for quality assessment (~8 per language pair), and fundamental disagreements about annotation strategy (Figures 8-9) suggest task ambiguity
Dataset critically small at only 224 documents with minimal expert annotation; 11 documents removed as 'faulty' without transparent criteria or detailed analysis

Severe scope limitations: only high-resource, closely related languages with Latin scripts; acknowledged impossibility to generalize to typologically distant languages or non-Latin scripts severely limits impact

Extreme performance drops may indicate annotation quality issues rather than dataset realism; unexplained label distribution differences (10-17% vs 25-30% different tokens) could explain performance gaps but are not investigated

Methodological issues: selection bias in choosing only 'best' LLMs for SwissGov evaluation due to computational constraints; reduced iSTS-RSD evaluation (100 vs full samples); LLM output failures on 7.4% of SwissGov examples (Table 4)

No clear error analysis explaining why absolute performance is so poor (best ~12-25 correlation); raises questions whether benchmark is well-defined or whether annotation ambiguity is primary limitation

Limited novelty: RSD task from prior work; main contribution is the dataset but its quality is compromised; benchmarking existing systems provides limited new insights beyond 'real data is harder than synthetic data'

strengths: Novel, well-motivated dataset addressing a genuine gap: first naturally-occurring, document-level, cross-lingual RSD benchmark with practical utility for multilingual content alignment
Comprehensive evaluation across diverse model types (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoders) with both open and closed-source systems

Important finding: demonstrates substantial generalization gap (up to 78-point Spearman difference) between synthetic iSTS-RSD and naturalistic SwissGov-RSD, with clear implications for dataset design
Rigorous dataset construction: two-phase annotation with feedback, clear labeling scheme, manual validation, thoughtful removal of faulty documents, and detailed guidelines
Strong reproducibility: promised code/data release, comprehensive hyperparameters and annotation guidelines in appendices, and clear methodology
Insightful qualitative analyses: document length effects (Figure 5), LLM underlabeling tendency, and system-specific failure modes provide interpretable findings
weaknesses: Uneven annotation quality across language pairs, particularly for EN-DE (IoU 11.17/10.22, F1 18.09/17.22) compared to EN-FR/EN-IT, with systematic annotator disagreement on span boundaries and handling of omissions/additions documented in Appendix A.4. Table 7 shows model ranking instability by annotator, especially for EN-DE
Limited dataset scale (224 documents with only 25 for agreement measurement) and severely imbalanced label distribution (10-17% positive) reduce robustness and generalization potential

Restricted language and script scope: only three closely-related European languages, all English-centric, with no typologically distant or non-Latin-script coverage, limiting generalizability of findings

Methodological bias in evaluation: selective LLM testing (only 'best-performing systems on iSTS-RSD' evaluated on SwissGov due to computational constraints), creating systematic disadvantage for methods not optimized on synthetic data; additional concerns include heuristic JSON fixes for malformed LLM outputs without impact analysis and noise from GPT-4o-mini label projection (34-46% samples edited)

Insufficient analysis depth: limited error analysis (single qualitative example), no investigation of linguistic phenomena causing failures, missing explanation for EN-IT's superior annotation agreement, no breakdown by difference types (omissions vs. paraphrases), and minimal practical guidance for practitioners

Incomplete experimental design: only comparison to one synthetic benchmark; different augmentation counts for LLMs (560) vs. encoders (10,000) complicates direct comparison; impact of LLM output format failures (Table 4) not analyzed despite increased frequency on SwissGov

strengths: Addresses practical real-world problem with compelling motivating examples (multilingual government content alignment)
Naturalistic dataset with real semantic differences, addressing limitations of synthetic iSTS-RSD benchmark
Comprehensive benchmarking of 25+ approaches (unsupervised, few-shot LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, encoders)
Important empirical finding: substantial performance gap (up to 78 Spearman correlation points) between synthetic and realistic settings
Meticulous documentation of annotation process with detailed guidelines, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and transparent methodology
Strong reproducibility: code/data promised for release, complete implementation details and hyperparameters provided
Systematic evaluation revealing specific failure modes (LLM output format errors, document length sensitivity, underlabeling toward document ends)
weaknesses: Inter-annotator agreement is modest (Spearman 43.61–65.09; mean IoU 23.98–32.10), raising concerns about gold standard quality for a token-level task
Severely limited scope: only 3 closely-related European languages, Latin scripts, English-centric pairs, government domain; generalizability to other languages and domains unclear
Dataset size modest (~186K tokens per language pair, 224 documents total); small for modern deep learning and limited to two annotators per pair
Task formulation under-specified: cross-lingual token alignment procedure not clearly described; handling of tokenization differences across languages not discussed
Extremely low overall performance (best Spearman ~6–7 on SwissGov-RSD) limits insights into solvability; no human performance baseline for reference
No novel methodological contributions: paper benchmarks existing approaches without proposing methods tailored to document-level cross-lingual RSD
Limited error analysis: no systematic study of challenging linguistic phenomena, error types by model, or linguistic drivers of semantic differences
Label projection introduces potential biases: only 50 samples per language pair manually verified; impact on model performance not studied
Evaluation metric not justified: Spearman correlation assumes ordered scale, but semantic differences may be categorical; alternative metrics not explored
LLM prompting not optimized: simple uniform prompts acknowledged as limiting, but sophisticated strategies (example selection, iterative refinement) not explored

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical problem with high relevance for multilingual content management and government websites
Introduces a naturalistic dataset with real semantic differences, addressing limitations of synthetically augmented iSTS-RSD
Comprehensive evaluation spanning diverse systems: multiple LLMs (Llama, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) and encoder models (XLM-R, LaBSE, ModernBERT variants) with multiple settings
Transparent and well-documented annotation process with detailed guidelines, inter-annotator agreement metrics, and two-phase validation protocol
Clear empirical finding: substantial performance gap (up to 78 Spearman points) between synthetic and naturalistic data, providing useful reality check for the field
Strong reproducibility support through extensive appendices, promised code/data release, and detailed hyperparameters
Analysis of model behavior across document lengths (Figure 5) provides insights into LLM limitations on extended inputs
weaknesses: Moderate inter-annotator agreement undermines gold standard quality: Spearman correlation ranges 43.61-65.09 (EN-FR to EN-IT); token-level F1 scores 33-55% suggest substantial annotator disagreement
Post-hoc annotation replacement (footnote 6) and subjective manual merging of disagreements introduce bias; no release of both annotators' versions limits reproducibility of this decision
Dataset size is limited (224 documents, 886 texts) compared to modern standards; iSTS-RSD training set has 2800 pairs + augmentations, limiting statistical robustness and fine-tuning effectiveness

Language scope is highly restricted: only closely related European languages with Latin scripts; generalizability to distant language pairs, low-resource languages, or non-Latin scripts is completely unexplored
Insufficient error analysis: only two examples shown (Figure 4); lacks systematic categorization of difference types, linguistic phenomena causing failures, or root cause analysis of performance gaps

Performance gap explanation is shallow: paper demonstrates systems fail on real data but doesn't investigate whether gap stems from realism, document length, label skew (10-17% vs 25-30%), or other factors

Label projection quality (Section 4.4) is inadequately validated: only 50 samples per language pair manually checked; systematic noise in projected labels propagating through fine-tuning is not thoroughly analyzed
No novel methods proposed: paper applies existing approaches to new benchmark without architectural innovations or methodological contributions; core finding (synthetic ≠ real) is unsurprising
No actionable solutions or deep insights: paper identifies failures but provides no guidance for practitioners or future researchers; conclusion mentions 'specialized approaches' without elaboration
Incomplete LLM evaluation on SwissGov-RSD due to computational constraints: only best-performing systems from iSTS-RSD evaluated, preventing fair assessment of which LLMs suit real data

Experimental design issues: different augmentation strategies and training setups for different model types complicate fair comparison; statistical significance testing and confidence intervals are absent

Dataset not systematically characterized: lacks structured analysis of difference types, domain breakdown beyond government context, or linguistic phenomena distribution despite complexity shown in examples

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing real discrepancies in multilingual government content
High-quality, naturalistic dataset with systematic two-phase annotation process and transparent quality control (inter-annotator agreement metrics, overlap validation)
Comprehensive benchmarking covering diverse systems (unsupervised, LLMs, encoders) across multiple settings (few-shot, fine-tuning, label projection)
Important empirical finding: substantial performance gap (up to 78 points Spearman) between synthetic iSTS-RSD and naturalistic SwissGov-RSD, with implications for evaluation methodology
Systematic analysis of failure modes: document length effects on LLMs, formatting errors, comparative robustness of unsupervised approaches
Strong reproducibility: code and data publicly available, detailed hyperparameters, full annotation guidelines, example prompts in appendices
Methodological rigor: transparent handling of annotator replacement, honest limitations section, multiple evaluation metrics (Spearman, Kendall τ-b)
weaknesses: Limited language and script diversity: only high-resource, closely related European languages (Germanic/Romance) with Latin script; all pairs English-centric; generalizability to typologically distant or non-Latin-script languages untested

Moderate inter-annotator agreement particularly concerning for EN-FR (43.61 Spearman), with EN-DE requiring annotator replacement (initial 9.4 → 56.14), suggesting underlying quality issues; only 2 annotators per language pair
Relatively small dataset (224 documents per pair, 11 removed as faulty) limits statistical power; no learning curves or systematic analysis of scaling behavior

Incomplete analysis of performance gap: while paper demonstrates drop from iSTS-RSD to SwissGov-RSD, provides limited insight into root causes beyond 'naturalness'; missing error analysis comparing failure modes across datasets

Label distribution mismatch: 10-17% semantic differences in SwissGov-RSD vs. 25-30% in iSTS-RSD, potentially explaining part of performance gap independent of domain shift; reversed scale relative to iSTS complicates comparison
No statistical significance testing between reported model scores; confidence intervals absent; unclear which performance differences are meaningful given moderate inter-annotator agreement ceiling

LLM evaluation constraints: intentionally simple/uniform prompting limits exploration of prompt optimization; only best-performing systems evaluated on SwissGov-RSD for computational reasons; formatting error workarounds could introduce artifacts

Label projection introduces systematic bias: GPT-4o-mini-projected labels show 34-46% sample-level edits needed (1.72-3.50% token-level error), potentially skewing fine-tuned results; validation on only 50 samples per language pair
Limited methodological novelty: paper benchmarks existing approaches (DiffAlign, standard LLM prompting, encoder fine-tuning) without proposing new methods

Incomplete document-length analysis: Figure 5 shows qualitative trends only; missing quantitative correlation, length-specific fine-tuning investigations, and systematic performance degradation curves
